text: The *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") of Genesis 6 have one of the strangest interpretive histories in the reception of the Bible. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions (the Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads it as scripture), elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who descended to corrupt humanity in two ways: by forbidden teaching and by miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this angelic reading. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected it and favored the Sethite genealogy instead. On that view the sons of God are the godly line of Seth, and the daughters of men are the line of Cain. Other readers have set the passage beside ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The chapter also introduces the flood narrative, which belongs to a broader Mesopotamian tradition. That tradition is preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and in tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative), and both contain close parallels to the biblical flood story. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds is *tevah* ("ark," "chest"). Scripture uses it elsewhere only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
